C.description: Researchers reconstruct past societies by authenticating documents, dating records, interpreting inscriptions, coins, seals, and symbols, and tracing institutional, familial, and material evidence through archival and archaeological methods.

CD.description: Researchers authenticate and interpret historical documents, examining their creation, transmission, preservation, material features, and official marks to establish provenance, authority, and evidentiary value.

D.description: Researchers reconstruct European and Mediterranean pasts through archival documents, material remains, political institutions, and cultural practices, comparing regional change from antiquity through modern national formations.

DK.description: Researchers reconstruct eastern European societies through archival records, travel accounts, landscapes, monuments, ethnographic observations, and studies of everyday customs, political change, and regional communities.

DR.description: Researchers reconstruct southeastern European pasts through archives, travel accounts, ethnographic observation, regional surveys, and serial publications, comparing political change, communities, landscapes, and everyday life across neighboring countries.

DS.description: Researchers reconstruct Asian societies and cultural change through archives, archaeology, languages, religious traditions, and comparative analysis across regions and diasporas.

DT.description: Researchers reconstruct African pasts through archival records, oral traditions, archaeology, colonial encounters, and political change across regions, societies, and periods.

E.description: Researchers reconstruct North and South American pasts by analyzing political institutions, social change, migration, conflict, and everyday life through archives, oral testimonies, material evidence, and comparative interpretation.

F.description: Researchers reconstruct societies across the Western Hemisphere by analyzing archives, oral traditions, political institutions, migration, colonization, and cultural change in communities shaped by European and Indigenous encounters.

G.description: Researchers examine Earth’s surfaces, oceans, and spatial relationships, producing and interpreting maps, globes, atlases, and quantitative representations through field observation and measurement.

GB.description: Researchers examine Earth’s surface processes, water movement, terrain formation, and hazards through field observation, mapping, measurement, modeling, and theoretical analysis.

GC.description: Researchers examine seawater, sediments, currents, seabed forms, and marine resources, using chemical analyses, physical measurements, regional comparisons, and underwater surveys to understand ocean processes and pollution.

GE.description: Researchers examine how human activities alter ecosystems, measure ecological conditions and risks, evaluate governance and education, and study public communication, ethical responsibilities, and equitable distribution of environmental harms.

GN.description: Researchers investigate human biological variation, cultural practices, ancient remains, and philosophical questions through fieldwork, excavation, comparative analysis, measurement, and theoretical synthesis.

GV.description: Researchers examine how people use free time for enjoyment, studying games, entertainment settings, participation patterns, cultural meanings, and social or psychological effects through observation, surveys, and historical analysis.

HA.description: Researchers analyze population counts and social measurements, developing quantitative methods to collect, evaluate, interpret, and compare evidence about societies, institutions, and demographic change.

HB.description: Researchers examine how births, deaths, migration, and household change shape economies, using statistical models and historical data to explain population trends, growth, recessions, and recoveries.

HC.description: Researchers examine how societies produce, distribute, and consume goods over time, analyzing resource use, markets, institutions, environmental constraints, and historical change through archival and quantitative evidence.

HD.description: Researchers examine how production, employment, workplaces, firms, and regional economies evolve, using statistical analysis and institutional comparison to explain productivity, inequality, organization, and development.

HE.description: Researchers examine how people and goods move and how messages travel, analyzing infrastructure, networks, regulation, technologies, and their economic and social effects across regions.

HF.description: Researchers examine cross-border exchange, pricing barriers, merchant organizations, and professional training through historical records, periodicals, institutional archives, and comparative economic analysis.

HG.description: Researchers examine how money is intermediated through banks, insurers, investment firms, and payment networks, analyzing risk, regulation, corporate decisions, markets, and services using quantitative and institutional methods.

HJ.description: Researchers examine how governments raise, borrow, allocate, and record money, evaluating tax systems, border collections, municipal budgets, spending decisions, debt management, financial reporting, and oversight practices.

HN.description: Researchers examine historical living conditions, inequality, poverty, reform movements, religious responses, neighborhood institutions, and global development through comparative evidence and social research methods.

HQ.description: Researchers examine intimate relationships, gender roles, household routines, sexual representation, bereavement, and practical wellbeing through social analysis, education, historical inquiry, and cultural interpretation.

HT.description: Researchers examine how people organize in cities and countryside, analyzing social inequality, community life, settlement patterns, and relationships between populations through surveys, demographic data, and fieldwork.

HV.description: Researchers examine harmful substance use, offending, disasters, and vulnerable populations through prevention programs, aid services, institutional responses, and evaluation of rehabilitation and legal interventions.

J.description: Researchers examine power, governing arrangements, constitutions, elections, bureaucracies, and competing ideas of authority through comparative analysis of regimes, institutions, and public decision-making.

JC.description: Researchers examine how collective power is organized across historical periods, using philosophical texts, institutions, maps, and territorial practices to explain sovereignty, borders, national identity, and governmental change.

JK.description: Researchers examine American governance, bureaucratic practice, constitutional development, and wartime governmental records through archival research, legal analysis, and historical comparison.

JN.description: Researchers compare how European states organize authority, administer public services, and develop governing institutions, using constitutional records, administrative documents, and historical analysis across national cases.

JV.description: Researchers examine overseas expansion and population movement through governmental records, demographic data, regional comparisons, and accounts of encounters between settlers, governing powers, and native communities.

JZ.description: Researchers explain cross-border power, diplomatic choices, and security cooperation by comparing state behavior, analyzing policy goals, and studying interactions among governments and autonomous organizations.

K.description: Researchers examine binding norms across societies and faiths, comparing interpretive traditions, reasoning from sacred texts, resolving disputes, and tracing how principles govern communal conduct.

KF.description: Researchers examine nationwide American statutes, judicial precedents, equitable doctrines, and court-developed principles, comparing how federal and state institutions create, interpret, and apply legal rules.

KZ.description: Researchers analyze cross-border obligations, treaty interpretation, state responsibility, international organizations, arbitration, and rulings from global tribunals to determine how shared legal norms govern interstate conduct.

L.description: Researchers examine how learning is organized and experienced, tracing its historical development, institutional practices, specialized support, student life, instructional materials, and national variations through archival and comparative study.

LA.description: Researchers trace how schooling evolved across eras and places, examining institutions, policies, curricula, teachers, learners, and communities through archival records, statistics, oral testimony, and comparative analysis.

LB.description: Researchers examine how people learn, how instruction should be organized, and how educational aims are justified, using classroom observation, comparative analysis, and philosophical argument.

LC.description: Researchers examine how learning is organized across age groups and abilities, studying access, inclusion, ethics, community participation, lifelong development, and educational experiences beyond conventional institutions.

ML.description: Researchers examine how individual performers and coordinated groups create, interpret, and evaluate musical works through rehearsal practices, live presentation, and comparative performance analysis.

N.description: Practitioners create and interpret visual forms, studying composition, materials, techniques, spatial structures, and ornamental purposes across images, objects, buildings, and crafted environments.

NA.description: Researchers examine how buildings and civic spaces are conceived, represented, ornamented, regulated, exhibited, and judged through drawings, competitions, historical comparisons, and urban design practices.

NX.description: Researchers compare creative practices across performance and image-making, examining how works combine movement, sound, narrative, staging, and visual form through historical, critical, and interpretive analysis.

PN.description: Scholars examine written and staged expression, tracing how narratives, speeches, personal records, and curated collections are composed, performed, circulated, and interpreted.

Q.description: Researchers investigate the natural world through quantitative reasoning, observation, experimentation, and classification, studying matter, forces, celestial bodies, Earth processes, living organisms, plants, animals, and bodily structure.

QA.description: Researchers investigate quantity, form, motion, and uncertainty using logical proof, symbolic manipulation, measurement devices, computational procedures, historical texts, numerical tables, and data-based inference.

QB.description: Researchers measure celestial positions and motions, develop observing instruments and computational models, investigate cosmic origins and structure, and produce calibrated predictions from observatory and nonvisual data.

QC.description: Researchers investigate matter and energy through measurement and mathematical modeling, examining forces, radiation, charged systems, atmospheric processes, temperature, and interactions at atomic and subatomic scales.

QD.description: Researchers investigate substances and reactions through synthesis, measurement, structural analysis, laboratory experimentation, theoretical modeling, historical study, and communication of results.

QE.description: Researchers reconstruct Earth’s history by analyzing rocks, minerals, fossils, sediments, and plant remains, using field observations and laboratory methods to explain changing environments and geological processes.

QH.description: Researchers investigate living organisms and their cells, heredity, reproduction, evolution, environments, and extraterrestrial conditions through laboratory experiments, field observations, comparative analysis, and specialized research techniques.

QK.description: Researchers investigate plant form, function, diversity, and relationships through field surveys, controlled experiments, microscopy, specimen collections, and ecological studies across environments.

QL.description: Researchers investigate animal diversity, body structures, evolutionary relationships, behavior, specimen preservation, and strategies for protecting threatened populations and their habitats through fieldwork and comparative analysis.

QP.description: Researchers investigate how animals function, examining organ systems, fluids, metabolism, nutrition, movement, circulation, and nervous control through laboratory experiments, measurements, and comparative studies.

R.description: Practitioners investigate human health and disease through clinical examination, laboratory testing, imaging, operative care, and prevention across organ systems and stages of life.

RA.description: Researchers examine how healthcare interacts with government and law, investigating disease prevention, environmental conditions, poisoning, geographic patterns, and medical evidence used in courts.

RC.description: Practitioners diagnose and manage adult and family health problems through patient histories, physical examinations, laboratory testing, preventive care, and evidence-based treatment across organ systems.

RD.description: Practitioners investigate disorders requiring operative correction, developing region-specific procedures, cancer removal, transplantation, anesthesia, and musculoskeletal reconstruction through clinical assessment, imaging, intervention, and outcomes research.

RG.description: Researchers investigate reproductive health across hormonal cycles, pregnancy, childbirth, and lactation, diagnosing and treating disorders affecting female reproductive organs, breasts, fertility, and endocrine regulation.

RJ.description: Researchers examine young people’s growth, development, disease, treatment, and wellbeing, using clinical observation, physiological measurements, preventive care, and age-specific health practices from infancy through adolescence.

RM.description: This field examines how illnesses respond to medicines, hormones, biological agents, nutrition, exercise, and rehabilitative interventions, emphasizing clinical evaluation, treatment delivery, and recovery.

S.description: Researchers examine how plants, trees, domesticated animals, and aquatic species are propagated, managed, harvested, and conserved, using ecological monitoring, breeding experiments, and resource-management practices.

SB.description: Researchers cultivate and improve edible, ornamental, and field-grown plants, investigating growth, landscape design, crop disorders, insect interactions, and practical garden management through experiments and observation.

SD.description: Researchers examine wooded landscapes, tree cultivation, harvesting, soils, conservation, governance, education, historical change, transport, and notable specimens through ecological, administrative, and applied fieldwork.

SF.description: This field examines animal care, breeding, behavior, and management across livestock, companion species, working creatures, domesticated birds, and economically useful insects through practical guidance and applied study.

SH.description: Researchers examine aquatic food production and harvesting, studying cultivated and wild species, catching practices, recreational participation, seafood supply chains, and publication-based communication.

SK.description: Researchers examine recreational pursuit of wild animals and aquatic species, studying tracking, capture techniques, equipment, environmental practices, regulations, and relationships between outdoor recreation and wildlife populations.

T.description: This field studies designing and maintaining infrastructure for water, transportation, and public health, using engineering analysis, materials testing, environmental assessment, and large-scale construction practices.

TA.description: Researchers design and test built infrastructure, optical systems, transport networks, and plasma devices, using surveying, material characterization, structural analysis, and fluid-dynamic experiments to solve practical problems.

TC.description: They study moving and storing water, designing dams, channels, irrigation systems, ports, and shoreline defenses through fluid mechanics, surveying, hydrologic analysis, and construction planning.

TD.description: Researchers design and evaluate systems that manage water, waste, pollution, and sanitation, measuring environmental exposures and engineering controls to protect communities and improve everyday living conditions.

TE.description: Researchers design, build, and maintain transport routes by testing surfacing materials, analyzing terrain and drainage, developing compaction machinery, and evaluating construction practices across regions and languages.

TH.description: Researchers examine how structures are assembled, serviced, illuminated, heated, ventilated, decorated, and protected from fire, using technical drawings, material specifications, and performance standards.

TJ.description: Researchers design, analyze, and manufacture machines, engines, boilers, pumps, locomotives, and industrial equipment, using mechanics, thermodynamics, fluid power, workshop practices, and regional applications.

TK.description: Researchers design and analyze circuits, generators, communication systems, power grids, lighting, household devices, and nuclear reactors using electromagnetic theory, materials science, and safety testing.

TL.description: Researchers design and analyze powered and human-propelled vehicles for roads, air, and space, studying propulsion, control, structural performance, and the engineering of mobile machines.

TN.description: Researchers extract and process ores, analyzing deposits, equipment, separation techniques, refining reactions, and industrial workflows to improve recovery, efficiency, safety, and environmental performance.

TP.description: Researchers develop industrial processes that transform raw materials into polymers, foods, ceramics, glass, fuels, dyes, and textiles, optimizing chemical reactions, thermal treatment, purification, and large-scale manufacturing.

TS.description: Researchers examine how raw materials become usable products, studying factory processes, tools, regional production patterns, and trade through technical analysis of metals, textiles, paper, wood, leather, and rubber.

TX.description: Researchers examine household management and meal provision through nutrition, culinary preparation, budgeting, dining service, lodging operations, and maintenance practices, comparing domestic routines with commercial hospitality settings.

U.description: It examines armed-force organization, strategic conditions, logistics, ground and armored operations, firepower, fortification, and the planning and conduct of warfare beyond Earth.

UA.description: Researchers examine how societies organize protection, movement, communication, and preparedness, analyzing strategic planning, geographic constraints, civilian resilience, and nonviolent responses through historical and contemporary evidence.

UB.description: Researchers examine how armed forces organize personnel, issue orders, maintain administrative records, manage service careers, support veterans, and investigate misconduct through official correspondence and reports.

UC.description: Researchers examine how military forces move, house, feed, equip, and maintain personnel and animals, analyzing administrative systems, supply chains, transport vehicles, camps, barracks, and field support practices.

UF.description: This field examines weapon design, ammunition, projectile motion, explosive performance, firing instruments, targeting procedures, and the training documents governing their battlefield use.

UG.description: Researchers examine how armed forces operate in air and near-Earth environments, studying vehicle technologies, detection systems, fortifications, training rules, tactical doctrine, and defensive responses to missiles.

UH.description: Researchers examine how armed forces provide healthcare, spiritual support, animal assistance, morale activities, sanitation, and aid to personnel and communities through institutional records and operational studies.

V.description: Researchers examine maritime forces and commercial shipping through fleet organization, strategic deployment, administration, personnel systems, vessel upkeep and design, weapons, navigation, and supporting services.

VA.description: Researchers examine how sea forces are structured, funded, distributed, and mobilized, comparing global fleets, reserve systems, maritime readiness, and the logistical consequences of naval policy.

VC.description: It examines how maritime forces sustain personnel and vessels through logistics, budgeting, inventories, recordkeeping, transport networks, procurement, and management of bases and repair facilities.

VE.description: Researchers examine the organization, training, matériel, living conditions, honors, and historical development of military forces through regulations, instructional texts, technical records, and collected accounts.

VG.description: This field examines naval support operations, personnel welfare, communications, religious provision, bands, postal systems, coastal protection, and aviation through administrative and historical analysis.

VK.description: Researchers study how commercial vessels determine position and course, applying geometry, instrumentation, chart interpretation, and error analysis to improve safe, efficient passage at sea.

VM.description: Researchers design and analyze watercraft, studying hull behavior, construction practices, propulsion systems, onboard power, shipyard production, and specialized vessels through engineering calculations and practical testing.

Z.description: Researchers organize, describe, preserve, and interpret written records, studying book production, handwriting, publishing networks, cataloging practices, and how collections provide access to knowledge.
